title: Stream first-response & kernel check-in
summary: Weekly pilot check-in focusing on first-response (TTFT) and streaming behavior for StratoHealth's clinical summarization flow. Reviewed kernel selection effects across seqlen distributions, microburst behavior, and hedging options. Agreed to run a dedicated microburst profile, share kernel perf sheet, and trial a hybrid streaming + small-batch config on dedicated nodes next week.
next_steps: Redwood to upload kernel performance spreadsheet to shared drive by 2027-04-23
StratoHealth to run the microburst harness and share logs by 2027-04-26
Schedule deep-dive on quantized path with Samira for 2027-04-28
Agree on pilot success metrics and finalize canary policy by next sync
action_items: Jordan Lee: publish kernel perf spreadsheet (link placeholder) ; due 2027-04-23
Liam Chen: run microburst harness against dedicated node and attach trace logs ; due 2027-04-26
Samira Ahmad: prepare short demo of hybrid streaming + micro-batch config on staging ; due 2027-04-27
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-04-21 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Jordan Lee (Redwood SE), Samira Ahmad (Redwood SE), Maya Ortiz (CTO - StratoHealth), Liam Chen (Lead ML Eng), Priya Rao (Infra), Tom Alvarez (Product), Evan (SRE, dialed in)

Summary/Context: quick weekly pilot check-in. Main ask from customer: shave 10-30 ms off median TTFT for short clinical prompt completions and stabilize streaming jitter during 99th pct microbursts. They've been running on the hosted pilot but are testing dedicated nodes this week.

[00:00] Alex Kim: hey everyone, thanks for joining — will do a quick agenda. we want to review last week's metrics, go over kernel choices you tried, and agree on a short action list. Maya, you on?
[00:14] Maya Ortiz: yeah i'm here, sorry slight delay, had a quick infra standdown. hey team.
[00:19] Liam Chen: morning all, got the logs from last run — there's a bunch of small sequences like 8-12 tokens but then occasional 512 bursts for some long discharge notes.
[00:34] Jordan Lee: ok so that's the seqlen tail; thanks for sharing. before we dig in, quick note: when i say TTFT i mean time-to-first-token; sometimes our reports call it first-response.
[00:46] Priya Rao: yes please call it first-response, that's what our SREs logged. also, we're testing both hosted and dedicated today, hoping to observe differences.

[01:05] Samira Ahmad: quick reminder — on dedicated we can push a different kernel mix (the fast single-token path) and try a reduced KV caching retention window. there are tradeoffs, we discussed last week.
[01:20] Tom Alvarez: what do you mean by reduced KV retention? isn't caching always good?
[01:26] Jordan Lee: good q — for multi-turn clinical summaries, the KV cache can grow and increase memory pressure causing longer GC-ish stalls for certain runtimes. reducing retention on short sessions can give faster first tokens at the cost of re-computation later.

[01:56] Maya Ortiz: okay, show me the numbers. Liam, you said median TTFT is around 110 ms on hosted?
[02:05] Liam Chen: correct, median about 110 ms, p95 around 380 ms, p99 spikes to ~1.2s during the microbursts. the dedicated node run this morning showed median 92 ms but p99 still hit ~800 ms.
[02:23] Alex Kim: thanks — so median improvement with dedicated but tail still an issue. Jordan, can you walk through kernel differences we tried?

[02:38] Jordan Lee: sure — we experimented with three kernel sets: baseline full-precision gemm kernels (we call them fp-k1), quantized fused kernels (qf-k2) and a hybrid small-seq kernel (ss-k3) optimized for <=16 token outputs. On hosted the routing defaulted to fp-k1 for compatibility; on dedicated we forced ss-k3 for short sequences. The ss-k3 path gives ~20-30 ms improvement on median for sequences under 16 tokens.
[03:09] Maya Ortiz: that matches what we saw. the weird part is the p99 not falling as much — seems bursty.
[03:18] Jordan Lee: right — the bursts are often from background retrains or other tenants on shared racks, but on dedicated we still saw internal microbursting due to serialization on the streaming pipeline.
[03:33] Liam Chen: i pulled traces — the backend shows small queuing delays when we flush the streaming buffer; sometimes the streamer batches multiple small requests and then serializes output writes.

[03:55] Samira Ahmad: two levers: reduce streaming flush window (more frequent flushes) or enable a low-latency hedging path that duplicates the first token to an alternate kernel and cancels on success. Hedging costs tokens but can recover p99.
[04:12] Priya Rao: hedging sounds expensive — we care about cost too. do you have an estimate?
[04:20] Jordan Lee: rough math: hedging the first token doubles early compute for maybe 5-7% added token cost on these workloads because many sessions are short. But we can limit hedges to sessions predicted to hit microbursts (we have heuristics from sequence history).

[04:49] Tom Alvarez: can you detect microburst-prone sessions reliably?
[04:53] Samira Ahmad: not perfect but decent — if previous session or current prompt has a long context or attachments, we raise a 0.6 probability and then hedging only for those. we'll share the heuristics.

[05:15] Maya Ortiz: okay, i'd prefer heuristic hedging rather than blind hedging. plus can we try streaming flush tuning first — that might be lower-cost.
[05:25] Alex Kim: agreed. action item: try flush window at 10 ms, 25 ms, 50 ms on staging and compare p50/p95/p99. Jordan you'll set that up?
[05:34] Jordan Lee: yep — will run the three configs on dedicated staging.

[06:00] Evan (SRE): quick note — our infra team flagged that during the 800 ms spikes there were also kernel context-switch stalls at the hypervisor level; could be NUMA pinning or GPU scheduler preemption. Priya can we pin to isolated NUMA on the dedicated nodes?
[06:17] Priya Rao: we can try stricter NUMA affinity, yes. but that will reduce packing. for the pilot we can reserve nodes.

[06:35] Liam Chen: on quantization — the qf-k2 path reduced memory footprint but introduced small decoding jitter for long sequences; the hybrid path ss-k3 didn't support some fused op optimizations and so for very long seqlens we fallback to fp-k1. That fallback causes a compaction penalty which sometimes contributes to tail.
[06:58] Jordan Lee: exact — fallback transitions are expensive. our runtime can pre-warm alternative kernels if we can predict seqlen distribution per session, but that needs extra bookkeeping.
[07:16] Alex Kim: is prediction viable given Strato's traffic patterns?
[07:20] Liam Chen: yes-ish — most workflows are predictable by route: triage summaries are 8-20 tokens often, discharge notes are long. we can tag sessions at the API level so runtime knows target seqlen.
[07:36] Maya Ortiz: good, we'll add a seqlen_hint field in the next API call batch — that should help.

[07:50] Samira Ahmad: also want to call out prefix caching for repeated patient-context snippets — on some flows you can save ~10-15 ms if we cache prefix embeddings locally. But caching semantics must align with privacy constraints.
[08:07] Priya Rao: yes, but audit logs and KMS usage are critical. we need logs for any cached content and encrypted storage.
[08:16] Jordan Lee: Redwood supports KMS-backed cache encryption and audit logs in the console; we'll share the compliance doc.

[08:40] Tom Alvarez: on the dedicated run you referenced a reduced KV retention window — did that materially change p99?
[08:48] Liam Chen: modest effect on p50/p95, not on p99 — p99 is dominated by queuing and kernel fallbacks rather than cache evictions.

[09:05] Alex Kim: ok let's list experiments to run in parallel: (1) Streaming flush window sweep; (2) small first-token hedging on heuristic sessions; (3) seqlen_hint pre-warming to avoid fallback; (4) NUMA affinity isolation on dedicated nodes; (5) microburst harness run with kernel traces. Jordan to coordinate.

[09:30] Jordan Lee: noted. i will provision three dedicated staging nodes: one with default, one with NUMA isolated and ss-k3 forced for <=16 tokens, one with hedging enabled. will run a 4-hour microburst synthetic and the real traffic replay.
[09:48] Maya Ortiz: how do you want logs? we can attach flamegraphs and perf traces.
[09:53] Jordan Lee: perfect — flamegraphs + per-token timeline. also if you can include host-level scheduler traces that helps isolate hypervisor stalls.

[10:10] Liam Chen: i want to mention an oddity — we saw occasional token duplication in the stream when a hedged path returned concurrently. probably because the cancellation race wasn't clean in the client.
[10:22] Samira Ahmad: yep that's an implementation nuance — we should return only the earliest token and then emit cancel signals; we can send a client-side patch to handle dedupe.

[10:40] Alex Kim: make a note: client dedupe patch required if hedging enabled. Samira to draft.

[11:00] Maya Ortiz: about costs — can you quantify the expected token cost delta for a hedging strategy limited by heuristics?
[11:08] Jordan Lee: ballpark: 3-8% added compute cost depending on heuristic aggressiveness. we'll produce a runbook with cost estimates per policy.

[11:25] Priya Rao: SLA question: if we move to dedicated but use hedging and pre-warming, do we still get your standard latency SLOs?
[11:33] Alex Kim: yes, we can commit to revised SLOs for the dedicated pool. we'll reflect hedging behavior in the SLO calculation and adjust alert thresholds.

[11:50] Tom Alvarez: on quantization, are there quality regressions we should worry about for clinical text?
[11:57] Jordan Lee: small risk — qf-k2 tended to produce identical outputs for most prompts, but edge-case copying or precise numeric formatting could differ. we recommend running regression evals (we'll provide tests) before switching production.

[12:18] Liam Chen: we've got a small set of golden prompts and a test harness; will run that against qf-k2 and ss-k3 and post diffs.

[12:32] Maya Ortiz: ok great. also, can Redwood instrument per-route token breakdowns? we want to tie cost back to product features.
[12:40] Alex Kim: yes, Redwood Console has per-route token/cost; we'll add the StratoHealth routes and share initial breakdown by Friday.

[12:55] Evan (SRE): one more infra note — during morning runs we saw GPU temperature throttling on one chassis; might be causing periodic slowdowns. Priya to follow up with infra ops.
[13:07] Priya Rao: noted, we'll rotate the chassis out during the next test.

[13:20] Samira Ahmad: recap of experiments and owners: Jordan will run flush window sweep + hedging + pre-warm tests; Liam will run microburst harness and golden-prompt regression; Samira will prototype client dedupe + hybrid streaming demo; Alex will produce SLO adjustments and cost estimates.

[13:45] Tom Alvarez: can we target the next check-in for one week? same time next Wednesday?
[13:50] Maya Ortiz: works for me.

[14:02] Alex Kim: perfect — next meeting 2027-04-28 15:00 UTC. i'll send calendar invite and attach the kernel perf spreadsheet when Jordan uploads.

[14:15] Maya Ortiz: thanks everyone, appreciate the progress. quick Q: any blockers on compliance review if we move caches to KMS?
[14:23] Jordan Lee: nothing we haven't documented; we'll push SOC2 docs and the KMS integration notes.

[14:35] Maya Ortiz: ok thanks.

End transcript.
